summary: Glue records give the addresses of name servers that live inside the zone they serve, so resolvers can find them. This document clarifies that authoritative servers should return all available in-domain glue in referral responses. If it does not fit, the server must set the TC (truncated) bit so the client retries over another transport. It updates RFC 1034.

eli5.summary: If directions to a house are on a map inside the house, you can't find the house. Glue puts a note outside. If the note is too long, say "too long, ask again with a bigger page."

questions: when to set tc bit dns referral
when must a dns server set the tc flag
what is sibling glue in dns
subtitle: When a DNS referral cannot fit all the in-domain glue, the server must say so with the TC flag.

tldr.problem: A referral that leaves out the address of a name server inside the delegated zone leaves the resolver unable to follow it, and some servers did this without setting the TC flag.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires a server to put all available in-domain glue in the additional section, or to set TC=1 when message size prevents it. Sibling glue is a SHOULD, with TC=1 optional.
tldr.outcome: This updates RFC 1034 and may raise the share of UDP responses with TC set, and so the number of TCP queries.

today: RFC 9471 is a Proposed Standard from September 2023 that updates RFC 1034. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Glue Exists
sections.content:
Glue records are address records (A or AAAA) kept in a parent zone for name servers that live inside the zone being delegated. They are returned in referral responses; otherwise a resolver following the referral has no way of finding those addresses. At the time of writing they are the only type of glue defined for the DNS.

Authoritative servers are expected to return all available glue for in-domain name servers. If message size constraints prevent that over the chosen transport, the server MUST set the TC (Truncated) flag so the client knows the response is incomplete and SHOULD use another transport. This RFC clarifies that expectation.

It also points out that in-domain glue is not optional additional data, unlike some other content in the additional section. TSIG, OPT and SIG(0) are other extensions that are not optional when used.
sections.eli5: Glue is a small note that tells you where a helper lives when the helper's address would otherwise be locked inside the very place you are trying to reach.

sections.title: What the RFC Does Not Change
sections.content:
The document only clarifies requirements for name server software. It does not change any requirement about data placed in DNS zones or registries. The requirements apply to available glue records, those given in a zone, and say nothing about whether they are present in the zone.

If some glue is absent from a zone, an authoritative server may be unable to return a useful referral for the domain. The RFC says the IETF may want to consider a separate update on that.
sections.eli5: The rule is about handing over the notes you already have. It does not say who has to write the notes in the first place.

sections.title: Kinds of Glue in a Referral
sections.content:
The type of glue depends on the QNAME. The same name server can be in-domain for one response and a sibling for another.

  • In-domain: the name servers are below the delegation point. For foo.test delegated from test, the servers ns1.foo.test and ns2.foo.test need glue in the test zone.
  • Sibling: the name servers sit in another zone delegated from the same parent. Glue is often not strictly needed, because the resolver can follow up with the sibling zone, but most implementations include it as an optimization.
  • Cyclic sibling: each of two domains uses name servers under the other. This loop can only be broken if the delegating server includes the sibling glue in the referral.

In late 2021 the authors analyzed zone file data from ICANN's Centralized Zone Data Service and found 222 out of approximately 209,000,000 total delegations with only cyclic sibling NS records.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the helper lives in your own house, sometimes next door. If two neighbours each say the other one has the key, someone must write the address on the door.

sections.title: The Requirements
sections.content:
For in-domain name servers, a server generating a referral MUST include all available glue in the additional section, or MUST set TC=1 if constrained by message size.

For sibling name servers, it SHOULD include all available glue. If, after adding in-domain glue, the sibling glue does not fit, the server MAY set TC=1 but is not obligated to. Users may see failures for domains with cyclically dependent sibling servers when the glue is omitted, though the RFC notes such domains are rare.

Most iterative clients send initial queries over UDP and retry over TCP when TC is set. UDP responses are generally limited to between 1232 and 4096 bytes because of common EDNS0 UDP Message Size values, while TCP responses are limited to 65,535 bytes.
sections.eli5: If the note about someone living in the house does not fit, you must shout 'too long, ask again'. For neighbours' notes, shouting is allowed but not required.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 1034
sections.content: The RFC replaces one step of the referral algorithm in RFC 1034. The old text said to put whatever addresses are available into the additional section. The new text says to put whatever NS addresses are available there, and adds a sentence: if all glue RRs for in-domain name servers do not fit, set TC=1 in the header. Then go to step 4 as before.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook said 'write down what you can'. The new one adds 'and if you cannot fit the important ones, tell them'.

sections.title: Missing Glue in the Wild
sections.content:
The RFC includes an example of a response that lacks required glue with TC=0, which it says has been shown to cause resolution failures. It is based on a response observed in June 2020, with names changed to documentation domains. None of the glue records in the zone fit into the available UDP space, the TC flag was not set, and the authority section held NS and DS records but no addresses.

The servers originally responsible have since been updated and now set TC correctly. The RFC notes that the behavior has been seen with plain DNS responses too, not only DNSSEC ones.
sections.eli5: A helper handed over a list of names but no addresses and did not say the list was cut short. The person could not go on.

sections.title: Operational and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says most server implementations today set TC only when none of the available glue fits in a UDP response. The new requirements might therefore increase the fraction of UDP responses with TC set, and so the number of queries arriving over TCP.

On security, the RFC says it clarifies correct server behavior and does not introduce any changes or new security considerations. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: Telling people 'ask again' more often means more people come back for a second try, so the helper gets busier.
